title: Bridging customer scripts to inference harness - POC kickoff
summary: POC scoping focused on integrating Echelon's customer scripts with Redwood's benchmark harness. Primary goals: define success criteria (latency, p99, throughput), choose streaming vs non-streaming workloads for acceptance, map customer scripts to harness adapters, identify telemetry and pass/fail gates, and agree timeline for 3-week pilot with two benchmark runs.
next_steps: Redwood to share harness adapter template and example mapping (by 2026-01-26)
Customer to provide a representative sample of 200 customer prompts and a streaming client example (by 2026-01-25)
Set up shared Slack channel and access to test cluster credentials (ASAP)
action_items: Sofia - send harness adapter template + short doc - due 2026-01-26
Priya - export and share 200 sample prompts plus expected labels - due 2026-01-25
Marco - provision sandbox with Redwood test model and baseline config - due 2026-01-28
Tom - provide network topology and egress rules for VPC peering - due 2026-01-27
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-01-22
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Helen (Redwood SE), Luis (Redwood Eng), Priya (Echelon Head of ML), Tom (SRE), Anya (Data Scientist), Marcus (Platform), Kelsey (Procurement)

Auto-summary: kickoff scoping for POC harness integration focused on Echelon customer scripts. Decided on two-phase benchmark: initial non-streaming baseline, then streaming tests for low-latency traffic. Telemetry keys: p50/p95/p99, tail-latency, tokens/sec, model variant fallbacks, error rates.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Sofia Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick round of intros, and then we'll jump into the script integration stuff. Marco and Helen are our SEs who'll own the harness work.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Hi, I'm Priya. I own ML at Echelon. We're trying to validate the inference economics and tail latency for our personalization engine. We use a mixture of short prompts and some long context sessions.
[00:29] Tom Reynolds: Tom here, I'll help with infra and network. We've got a VPC in GCP and we want to avoid wide-open egress.
[00:34] Marcus Bell: Marcus, platform. We'll be mapping the traffic shapes and taking the runbook.
[00:40] Marco Li: Cool. Quick agenda: success criteria, workload size and shapes, how your scripts map to our harness, streaming vs batch decisions, telemetry, and timeline.
[00:49] Anya Kaur: Real quick - our prompts are conversational-ish, a lot of product recommendation context, sometimes we append user history (2-5 turns). We care a lot about p99 and cost per 1k completions.
[01:05] Helen Ortiz: When you say "user history", is that appended as a single context blob or streamed in multiple calls?
[01:09] Anya Kaur: At the moment we append as a single request. But we're exploring streaming to reduce latency on the tail.
[01:15] Luis Moreno: That's an important callout. Streaming changes both client integration and the harness. We'll want both flows in the POC.
[01:21] Priya Nair: Yeah, we want to see the delta. If streaming saves p99 by 200-300ms but costs x% more, we need to quantify that.
[01:31] Sofia Patel: Ok, success criteria idea: p50/p95/p99 thresholds per workload, mean tokens/sec, and cost delta vs baseline. Also an availability gate - errors under 0.5%. Does that align?
[01:42] Marcus Bell: Yes. Can we define concrete numbers? For example, p99 < 600ms for short prompts, p99 < 1.2s for long contexts?
[01:50] Priya Nair: Those are reasonable starting points. For business acceptance, p99 under 800ms for short is preferable. If streaming gets us to 600ms that's a win.
[01:59] Marco Li: We'll propose acceptance gates in the harness config so runs are automatically marked pass/fail. We'll include tokens cost per 1k, and an ops-level SLA check.
[02:08] Tom Reynolds: On the network side, we'll need an IP allowlist and SAML-based access. We'll also want to test with private egress and VPC peering to your dedicated environment if feasible.
[02:17] Helen Ortiz: For the harness integration, the common pattern is writing an adapter that translates your customer script into our runner format — we call it an 'adapter shim'. We'll share a template.
[02:27] Priya Nair: Sounds good. Our scripts are python-based, using asyncio and websockets for streaming.
[02:33] Marco Li: Perfect, that's one of the patterns we've supported. One caveat: some of the websocket client libraries implement back-pressure differently — we should capture that in the adapter.
[02:43] Anya Kaur: Also, some of our prompts expect partial decoding callbacks (we stream partial tokens to UX). Will the harness support measuring partial latency?
[02:51] Helen Ortiz: We can instrument partial callback timing; it's not standard in every benchmark but we can add hooks. We usually log first-token time, last-token time, and token throughput.
[03:02] Sofia Patel: Let's talk about workload sizing: Anya, can you outline your traffic mix? Short vs long, concurrency, and typical QPS?
[03:09] Anya Kaur: We have two main workloads: recommendations (short, avg 40 tokens, peak 400 qps), and conversation sessions (long, avg 600 tokens, peak 40 concurrent sessions, bursts up to 120).
[03:22] Marco Li: Good—this suggests two benchmark profiles: a high QPS non-streaming profile to validate throughput/cost, and a streaming session profile to validate tail latency under concurrent session behavior.
[03:33] Priya Nair: For the high QPS test, we want to run sustained 10-minute windows at peak load and collect p50/p95/p99. For the streaming sessions, we'll run mixes of concurrency with ramp-up to see tail behavior.
[03:45] Marcus Bell: Ramp-up plan noted. What about warm cache? We saw earlier calls about KV cache and cold starts. We'll want cold-start passes and warmed passes.
[03:54] Luis Moreno: Right, warm vs cold is part of acceptance. We'll do an initial cold run (simulate 0 warm KV cache) and then a warmed run after 15 minutes of steady traffic. That'll show the delta and cold-start tail.
[04:05] Tom Reynolds: On telemetry, we need export of tracing spans and token-level metrics. Can you confirm Redwood exposes per-request trace IDs?
[04:12] Marco Li: Yes, we can include trace IDs and payload-level tags. We recommend adding your correlation IDs in the adapter. Our dashboard can ingest traces and show per-route breakdown.
[04:21] Anya Kaur: Great. Also, we want model fallback behavior: if primary model variant is saturated, does Redwood auto-fallback to smaller quantized variant? How is that marked in metrics?
[04:31] Helen Ortiz: We can simulate fallback and flag fallback events in the run output. We'll mark those as pass/fail depending on your acceptance policy.
[04:39] Priya Nair: For cost calc, please include model tokenization delta, and GPU time cost. We'll need a token-level cost model from you.
[04:46] Sofia Patel: We'll provide a simple cost model mapping tokens and GPU-minutes to a per-1k completions metric. We'll also log GPU utilization.
[04:53] Marcus Bell: Regarding the harness, will you run the harness in our VPC or in Redwood's sandbox?
[04:58] Marco Li: We typically run the harness driver from a Redwood-managed runner for speed of iteration, but for HIPAA/regulatory-sensitive cases we can run the harness driver inside your VPC and connect to the private deployment. For this POC we can start Redwood-managed and then repeat in your VPC if needed.
[05:12] Tom Reynolds: Starting with Redwood-managed is fine as long as we test VPC peering later.
[05:16] Sofia Patel: Ok timeline proposal: week 0 (this week) - exchange scripts and sample prompts; week 1 - adapter integration and baseline non-streaming run; week 2 - streaming adapter and streaming run; week 3 - wrap-up, compare runs and produce acceptance report. Any objections?
[05:30] Priya Nair: That timeline works for us. Might need some slack if network peering is required.
[05:35] Marcus Bell: Agreed. Also please include a run to validate cold-start under a sudden burst — that's critical for our UX.
[05:43] Marco Li: We'll add a spike test case: 0 QPS to 100% load in 30s and measure tail.
[05:49] Anya Kaur: Quick question on adapter complexity. If our scripts call internal APIs to fetch user history, do you want us to stub those calls or let the harness mock them?
[05:58] Helen Ortiz: We prefer stubbing on your side or providing a sandbox endpoint. The harness expects deterministic inputs. If folks want to instrument real calls, we can do a separate integration test but it complicates reproducibility.
[06:10] Priya Nair: We'll provide a small mock service and an alternative where history is embedded in the request for deterministic runs.
[06:16] Sofia Patel: Good. On the subject of streaming vs non-streaming, tradeoffs we should weigh: streaming lowers time-to-first-byte and can reduce p99 for longer contexts, but often complicates client logic and can increase resource overhead due to more frequent context switching. We'll quantify both.
[06:33] Luis Moreno: Also mention memory usage on GPU for long contexts — might push us into a larger footprint and impact throughput. That will show up in GPU utilization.
[06:41] Tom Reynolds: For the streaming run, we want to measure first-token latency, partial token rates, and the time to first meaningful content for UX.
[06:50] Marco Li: We'll add those metrics. We'll also capture percent of sessions with early cancellation and how cancellations affect throughput and KV cache.
[06:58] Anya Kaur: One more thing — does the harness support token-level scoring so we can compute offline NLL or other ngram metrics? We want to validate quality doesn't regress when quantized variants are used.
[07:09] Helen Ortiz: Yes, we can include log-prob outputs and basic scoring, though log-probs may be approximated depending on model variant. We'll annotate runs with quality metrics and flag significant deltas.
[07:19] Priya Nair: Ok, let's capture acceptance: pass if (1) p99 short prompts < 800ms non-streaming baseline or < 600ms streaming run, (2) error rate < 0.5%, (3) quality delta (perplexity or NLL) within 5% of baseline, (4) cost per 1k completions within agreed budget.
[07:36] Sofia Patel: I'll draft those into the harness gate config and share.
[07:40] Marcus Bell: Networking: to enable Redwood-managed harness hitting your staging cluster, we'll need a short-lived service account and an allowlist. Tom will set the firewall rules.
[07:49] Tom Reynolds: I'll create an allowlist and will share a low-privilege service account for the test runner. Also, what about encryption keys? We want to ensure logs don't contain PII.
[07:58] Marco Li: We redact PII by default in traces for hosted runs and we can enable stricter redaction for this POC. For private runs in your VPC, data never leaves your network.
[08:07] Anya Kaur: Good, we'll aim to keep sample prompts anonymized.
[08:11] Kelsey: From procurement: what does the trial agreement look like? We need a short MSA addendum or trial SOW.
[08:17] Sofia Patel: We'll send a one-page SOW covering the test scope and data handling and a short trial MSA. Expect that by tomorrow.
[08:23] Kelsey: Great.
[08:26] Sofia Patel: Any other outstanding blockers?
[08:29] Priya Nair: Just confirm the example adapter language (python asyncio) and the sample prompt format.
[08:34] Marco Li: We'll send a python adapter and a node example. Also include a checklist: sample prompts (200), streaming client example, network allowlist, runbook for test harness.
[08:44] Sofia Patel: Let's recap next steps and owners.
[08:47] Sofia Patel: Redwood: send adapter template + harness mapping doc (Sofia) by 2026-01-26. Redwood: provision sandbox + baseline config (Marco) by 2026-01-28.
[08:57] Priya Nair: Echelon: share sample prompts and streaming client example (Priya/Anya) by 2026-01-25. Tom to provide allowlist details by 2026-01-27.
[09:09] Marcus Bell: We'll schedule the first run the week of Feb 2.
[09:13] Sofia Patel: Cool. Any final questions?
[09:16] Anya Kaur: None from me. Thanks.
[09:18] Tom Reynolds: Thanks all.
[09:19] Sofia Patel: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in Slack and with the docs. End call.

Post-call notes (auto):
- Agreed on two main benchmark profiles: high-QPS non-streaming and streaming session profile.
- Will execute cold and warmed runs, plus a stress spike test.
- Acceptance gates drafted above; Redwood to implement harness pass/fail logic.
- Security: PII redaction + allowlist for Redwood-managed runner; option to run harness in-customer VPC later.

References mentioned during call:
- Adapter template link (to be sent): /redwood/harness/adapter-template-python.md
- Example runbook (to be sent): /redwood/poc/runbooks/echelon-baseline.md

End of transcript.
